name: Multiple myeloma

matching.reasoningTemplate: Bone pain, anaemia, renal impairment and hypercalcaemia (CRAB) in an older patient suggests myeloma.

redFlags: Hypercalcaemia, renal failure, cord compression are emergencies (CRAB)

investigations.test: Serum/urine protein electrophoresis, free light chains

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e Ch.116 Plasma Cell Disorders, p.883-890 (PDF PAGE 926-933); hypercalcemia of malignancy Ch.57
clinicalPearls: Bone pain is the most common presenting symptom, affecting nearly 70% of patients; lesions are purely lytic (osteoblast suppression by DKK-1), so a radioisotope bone scan is LESS useful than plain radiography (p.886-887).
Serum alkaline phosphatase is typically NORMAL despite extensive bony disease because osteoblastic activity is suppressed (p.889).
Myeloma bone lesions are classically 'punched-out' lytic lesions (e.g. skull); diffuse osteopenia may also occur (p.887-889).
A reduced or negative anion gap may be a clue: the cationic M protein causes chloride retention; an associated pseudohyponatremia reflects reduced serum water from the high protein load (p.887).
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is characteristically elevated (p.889).

Urine dipstick is unreliable for light chains and the heat test for Bence Jones protein is falsely negative in ~50% of light-chain myeloma; a 24-h urine and serum free light chains are needed (p.888-889).
About 20% of myelomas secrete only light chains; <1% are truly non-secretory (M protein undetectable even by serum free light chain assay) (p.884, p.888-889).
Median age at diagnosis is ~69 years; uncommon under age 40; nearly twice the incidence in Black versus White populations; male predominance (p.885).

Susceptibility to infection is driven by hypogammaglobulinemia (of the non-M-component immunoglobulins), impaired antibody responses to polysaccharide antigens, and granulocyte/complement/T-cell dysfunction (p.886).
Most common infections are pneumonia (S. pneumoniae, S. aureus, K. pneumoniae) and pyelonephritis/UTI (E. coli and other gram-negatives) (p.886).
Renal light-chain cast nephropathy, light chain deposition disease, and AL amyloidosis are at least partially reversible with effective antimyeloma therapy (p.887).
Patients are prone to acute kidney injury when dehydrated or after iodinated contrast; NSAIDs and hypercalcemia further worsen renal function (p.887).
Plasma cell leukemia (>2000 circulating plasma cells/microL) is rare (~1%) but disproportionately frequent in IgD (12%) and IgE (25%) myeloma (p.889).
harrison.pathophysiology: Multiple myeloma is a malignant proliferation of a single plasma-cell clone. Myeloma cells adhere to bone marrow stromal cells and extracellular matrix, triggering cytokine loops (IL-6, IGF-1, VEGF) and signaling (Ras/Raf/MAPK, PI3K/Akt, PKC) that drive growth, survival, drug resistance, and migration. Osteoclast-activating factors (RANK ligand, MIP-1alpha, IL-1, lymphotoxin, TNF, VEGF) increase bone resorption while DKK-1 suppresses osteoblasts, producing purely lytic bone disease, hypercalcemia, fractures, and cord compression. The immune microenvironment is remodeled (expansion of MDSCs, plasmacytoid dendritic cells, TH17; suppression of effective antimyeloma T/B/NKT responses). Recurrent cytogenetic events include hyperdiploidy (trisomies) in ~half, and 14q32 IGH translocations [t(11;14), t(4;14), t(14;16)] in the rest, plus del13q, 1q amplification/1p deletion, and del17p; KRAS/NRAS are the most frequently mutated genes (~20% each), with TP53, DIS3, FAM46C, BRAF in 5-10%. No single unifying mutation exists; subclonal heterogeneity present at diagnosis drives genomic evolution. All myeloma is preceded by MGUS (p.883-885).
additionalDifferentials: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) - serum M protein <30 g/L, clonal marrow plasma cells <10%, no myeloma-defining events; ~1%/yr progression (p.887, Table 116-1)
Smoldering (asymptomatic) multiple myeloma - M protein >=30 g/L or urine M protein >=500 mg/24h and/or marrow plasma cells 10-60%, without myeloma-defining events (p.887-888, Table 116-1)
Solitary bone plasmacytoma and solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma (often younger patients; median survival >=10 years; M component in <30%) (p.888)
Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia / other IgM monoclonal gammopathies (p.883)
POEMS syndrome (polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, M-protein, skin changes; sclerotic bone lesions)

Reactive/secondary causes of an M component: CLL and B-/T-cell lymphomas, CML, breast and colon cancer, cirrhosis, sarcoidosis, parasitic disease, Gaucher disease, rheumatoid arthritis, myasthenia gravis, cold agglutinin disease, post-transplant (p.883)
nonInfectiousMimics: Metastatic carcinoma with lytic bone lesions (e.g. breast) (p.887)

Other causes of hypercalcemia of malignancy (PTHrP-mediated); myeloma must be specifically excluded with serum free light chains as ~3% are missed by serum/urine electrophoresis (Ch.57, p.349-350 region)
Other causes of marrow-infiltrative normocytic anemia in the elderly (p.886)
MGUS or smoldering myeloma misclassified as active disease without myeloma-defining events (p.887)
additionalInvestigations: Bone marrow aspirate AND core biopsy with kappa/lambda clonality (flow cytometry or immunohistochemistry); marrow plasma cells are CD138+ (p.887, Table 116-2)
Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation; quantitative IgG/IgA/IgM (p.888-889, Table 116-2)
Serum free light chains and involved:uninvolved ratio (p.888-889, Table 116-2)
24-h urine protein electrophoresis and immunofixation to quantify Bence Jones protein (p.888-889, Table 116-2)
Immunofixation for IgD or IgE in selected cases (p.889, Table 116-2)
Chemistry panel: calcium, creatinine/urea, uric acid; CBC; LDH (p.889, Table 116-2)
Serum beta-2-microglobulin and albumin for ISS staging (p.889, Table 116-2/116-3)
FISH or DNA sequencing for del17p/TP53, t(4;14), t(11;14), t(14;16), t(14;20), amp1q, del1p, del13 (p.889, Table 116-2/116-3)

Whole-body skeletal imaging: skeletal survey, low-dose CT, or 18F-FDG PET/CT (PET/CT standard to distinguish smoldering from active disease and to confirm solitary plasmacytoma); MRI spine/pelvis for marrow infiltration and cord/root compression (p.889, Table 116-2)
Serum viscosity if IgM, high IgA, or serum M component >7 g/dL (p.889, Table 116-2)
Abdominal fat-pad aspirate for amyloid in selected cases (p.889, Table 116-2)
redFlags: Spinal cord compression from vertebral collapse or plasmacytoma - radicular pain, loss of bowel/bladder control (oncologic emergency) (p.887)
Symptomatic hypercalcemia - lethargy, weakness, confusion, AKI (p.886-887)
Acute kidney injury, especially with dehydration, contrast, NSAIDs, or hypercalcemia (p.887)
Hyperviscosity syndrome - headache, visual disturbance, mucosal bleeding, somnolence, heart failure, retinopathy; symptoms above ~4 cP, most common with IgM > IgG3 > IgA (p.887)
Sepsis / serious bacterial infection (recurrent infection is the presenting feature in ~25%) (p.886)
harrison.prognosis: Serum beta-2-microglobulin is the single most powerful survival predictor; combined with albumin it defines the 3-stage International Staging System (ISS): Stage I (b2M <3.5 mg/L, albumin >=3.5 g/dL) median survival ~62 months; Stage II ~44 months; Stage III (b2M >5.5 mg/L) ~29 months. High LDH, circulating plasma cells, high labeling index, and poor performance status indicate worse outcome. Cytogenetic risk: high-risk = del(17p) (>=20% clonality)/TP53 mutation, t(4;14)/t(14;16)/t(14;20) with 1q gain or 1p deletion, biallelic/del1p with 1q gain, and high b2M with normal creatinine (~20-25% of patients, expected survival 3-4 years); standard-risk includes t(11;14), del(13), hyperdiploidy (~75-80%, survival 8-10+ years). del(13q) and t(11;14) are NOT high-risk markers. MGUS progresses ~1%/yr; SMM higher (high-risk SMM ~76% at 5 years). Solitary plasmacytomas carry median survival >=10 years. The Durie-Salmon system is no longer used (p.888-889).
pitfalls: Relying on urine dipstick (detects albumin, not light chains) or the Bence Jones heat test (false-negative ~50%) to exclude light-chain myeloma - use 24-h urine immunofixation and serum free light chains (p.888-889).
Excluding myeloma in hypercalcemia of malignancy without serum free light chains - ~3% of myeloma is missed by serum/urine electrophoresis with immunofixation.
Ordering a radionuclide bone scan instead of skeletal radiography/CT/PET-CT - lytic lesions lack osteoblastic activity and may be missed (p.887).
Misreading a normal alkaline phosphatase as evidence against bone disease (p.889).
Interpreting hyponatremia at face value - it is often pseudohyponatremia from high serum protein (p.887).
Labeling all monoclonal proteins as myeloma - M components occur in many neoplastic, autoimmune, and reactive conditions and require myeloma-defining events for the diagnosis (p.883, p.887).

Failing to distinguish MGUS/smoldering myeloma from active myeloma; active disease requires marrow clonal plasmacytosis (and/or plasmacytoma) plus a myeloma-defining event (CRAB or a malignancy biomarker).
harrison.severityClassification: Diagnosis (IMWG, Table 116-1): clonal marrow plasma cells (or biopsy-proven plasmacytoma) PLUS >=1 myeloma-defining event. CRAB end-organ damage: hyperCalcemia (>2.75 mmol/L or >0.25 mmol/L above ULN); Renal insufficiency (CrCl <40 mL/min or creatinine >177 micromol/L [>2 mg/dL]); Anemia (Hb <100 g/L or >20 g/L below LLN); Bone lesions (>=1 lytic lesion on radiograph/CT/PET-CT). SLiM biomarkers of malignancy (any one): clonal marrow plasma cells >=60%; involved:uninvolved serum free light chain ratio >=100; >1 focal lesion (>=5 mm) on MRI. Staging severity: International Staging System (ISS) I-III by serum beta-2-microglobulin and albumin; cytogenetic high-risk vs standard-risk further stratifies (R-ISS combines ISS with high-risk cytogenetics and LDH). MGUS = M protein <30 g/L, marrow plasma cells <10%, no myeloma-defining events; smoldering myeloma = M protein >=30 g/L (or urine >=500 mg/24h) and/or marrow plasma cells 10-60%, no myeloma-defining events (p.887-889).
